clue.text: A guy in a field

parts.note: a guy is a stuffed effigy of a man, and the one standing in a field keeps the birds off the crops

explanation.surface: Someone spots a fellow standing out in a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like any man, but in Britain a guy is a stuffed figure (as burnt on Guy Fawkes Night), and the one in a field is set up to frighten birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw-stuffed effigy posted among crops to frighten birds is exactly this figure.

clue.text: Dismisses part of the wind section, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us to listen to the word for the instrument, which sounds like another

parts.note: saxophones, sax for short, belong to an orchestra's wind section

explanation.surface: An orchestra lays off some of its woodwind players, rumour has it.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire an employee is to give them the sack.

clue.text: Stated that member entered into dubious deal

indicators.note: entered into means one piece goes inside another
a dubious deal is shady and suspect, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: Someone claimed that a club member was party to a shady agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests someone in a club, but here it is a limb of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Alleged means asserted or claimed, often without proof.

clue.text: That's Life!

parts.note: the familiar shrug of resignation, read literally as a definition of being alive

explanation.surface: A resigned shrug at a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation sounds like resignation, but read flatly it defines being alive.
explanation.definitionFit: Being, the state of being alive, is life.

clue.text: Lucifer thus ordered back in sporting revenge?

parts.note: to send something back is to return it
a lucifer is an old word for a friction match

explanation.surface: The devil, sent packing, gets his own back through sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lucifer' looks like Satan, but a lucifer was an early match; a match sent back is a 'return match'.
explanation.definitionFit: A second game giving the loser a chance to avenge defeat.

clue.text: Penelope's work never finished

annotationWithheld.why: Penelope's work never finished (3): the clue gives WEB (Penelope's endlessly unpicked weaving), which also gives BABYLON at 10-across, but the filed grid and answer read WEM, which nothing in the clue supports; the filed answer must be corrected first

clue.text: Oaks here in Surrey of course

definitions.text: Oaks here in Surrey of course

parts.words: Oaks here in Surrey of course
parts.note: the Oaks is a classic horse race run on a racecourse in Surrey, so 'of course' is literal

explanation.surface: Oak trees growing here in Surrey, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as 'naturally', but it means 'on a racecourse': the Oaks is a famous English flat race for fillies, run on the Surrey downs.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse town in Surrey that hosts the Oaks and the Derby.

clue.text: As did Barkis's 3 with the tide

annotationWithheld.why: As did Barkis's 3 with the tide (5): Barkis's life went out with the tide, so the clue gives EBBED (crossing BABYLON at 10-across), but the filed grid and answer read EARED, which the clue cannot give; the filed answer must be corrected first
annotationWithheld.clue: As did Barkis's 3 with the tide

clue.text: Tasty item in the seraglio

parts.note: both a dried grape, a tasty item, and a sultan's wife, who lives in the harem

explanation.surface: A delicacy found in the sultan's harem.
explanation.walkthrough: A seraglio is a harem; the word means a sultan's wife as well as a seedless raisin.
explanation.definitionFit: A seedless dried grape, and also a sultan's consort living in the harem.

clue.text: What do many in Church team, restructured, make of the opposition?

definitions.text: What do many in Church team, restructured, make of the opposition?

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, which is many
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: a team that is restructured is reorganised, so its letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Asking what a church side, once reorganised, will do to its rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: M is a thousand, so 'many'; 'restructured' turns TEAM into MEAT. To 'make mincemeat of' rivals is to beat them thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopped-up filling, as in the idiom for thrashing opponents completely.

clue.text: No knock-kneed player

parts.note: a musician who holds a large stringed instrument between the knees cannot keep them together

explanation.surface: A remark about a sportsman with straight legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests sport, but it is a musician whose instrument sits between parted knees.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of the large bowed instrument held upright between the knees.

clue.text: Miniature modern capital half destroyed by an ancient one

annotationWithheld.why: Miniature modern capital half destroyed by an ancient one (7): the clue gives BABYLON (BABY + LON, half of LONDON), but the filed MODEL answer MARILYN fits the filed crossers WEM and EARED, which are themselves wrong (WEB, EBBED); the grid can only be corrected all together
annotationWithheld.clue: Miniature modern capital half destroyed by an ancient one

clue.text: Sense of position, say

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the word for position and hear another word

parts.note: a site is a position or location

explanation.surface: A phrase meaning a feeling for where one stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision is one of the five senses.

clue.text: Make denial concerning my pudding diet

parts.note: re is a short word for concerning or about
read as 'pud I ate': PUD for pudding, and what I ate is my diet

explanation.surface: Someone protests about what their pudding-heavy eating says of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is loose by modern standards: 'my pudding diet' is the pudding (PUD) that I ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate is to disown or reject, to deny something firmly.

clue.text: These times not recorded short price I made

indicators.note: made here means made up, the letters put together in a new order

explanation.surface: A bargain price, invented by a shop assistant, is never written down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made' rearranges SHORT PRICE I.
explanation.definitionFit: The ages before written history have left no record.

clue.text: Evil product of a mad sort of rascal

parts.note: something evil is bad
the 'mad sort' is a hatter, as in the saying 'mad as a hatter', whose product is headgear

explanation.surface: Wickedness grows out of a crazy sort of scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'mad sort' is a hatter ('mad as a hatter', the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland), whose product is a HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned British expression for a scoundrel or ne'er-do-well.

clue.text: It can record a kind of game score

parts.note: a ball game, so ball can mean a kind of game
a point is a single score in a game

explanation.surface: Something that keeps the tally in a type of sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen with a tiny rolling ball tip, used for writing.

clue.text: A modern highwayman may need it to count the silver

definitions.text: A modern highwayman may need it

parts.note: to count is to number
a household's silver tableware is its plate

explanation.surface: A robber of today needs it to tot up the stolen silverware.
explanation.walkthrough: The modern highwayman robs by motor car, which carries a registration sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's registration plate, which a motorised robber's getaway vehicle must carry.

clue.text: The labour union heads in deep trouble, lots of it

indicators.note: deep trouble stirs things up, so these letters are rearranged
the heads of these three words are their first letters

explanation.surface: The trade union leaders are in serious difficulty, and plenty of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' takes TLU from 'The labour union'; 'trouble' rearranges it with IN DEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenitude is abundance, a full supply.

clue.text: A flower not connected with conflict

parts.note: something not fastened or attached is loose
strife is conflict or discord

explanation.surface: A bloom with no link to any quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall waterside plant with yellow or purple blooms.

clue.text: After work I had put in Peter, a townsman

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: put in means one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Peter Pan, the boy who never grew up
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: After a day's work, I had installed a man named Peter as a local resident.
explanation.walkthrough: An oppidan is a town dweller; at Eton College the word also means a boy who boards in the town rather than in college.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin for town, an oppidan is a town dweller.

clue.text: see 14 ac
Roman one Byron's gladiator helped to make

definitions.text: Roman one Byron's gladiator helped to make

parts.words: Roman one Byron's gladiator helped to make
parts.note: in Childe Harold, Byron's dying gladiator is 'butchered to make a Roman' festival day

explanation.surface: A literary allusion to a gladiator in Byron's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's line runs 'Butcher'd to make a Roman holiday'.
explanation.definitionFit: A day of public festivity and leisure, as the games were for Rome.

clue.text: Like a haggis or its jazzed-up accompaniment?

explanation.surface: Describing the Scottish pudding, or the lively music that goes with it.
explanation.walkthrough: A haggis (a Scottish savoury pudding) is served steaming and is traditionally piped in on bagpipes; jazzed-up piping is 'hot' music.
explanation.definitionFit: Served steaming from the pot, and bagpipe music made lively, as jazz is called hot.

clue.text: Nothing in leading feature gives criminal's fate

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the nose is the feature that leads, sticking out in front of the face
O, shaped like a zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: No prominent characteristic determines what becomes of a lawbreaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A hanging rope, the end of a condemned criminal.

clue.text: One big bid i' faith

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
in bridge a slam is a bid to win all or all but one of the tricks

explanation.surface: An archaic oath on making a large offer: 'One big bid, i' faith!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' faith' is an old oath (in faith) that hides the definition; 'i'' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The religion of Muslims is a faith.

clue.text: Would, say you, we get sugar from it?

definitions.text: Would, say you, we get sugar from it?

parts.words: Would, say you, we get sugar from it?
parts.note: 'Would, say you' means 'wood', spoken; a tree whose wood is known and whose sap is boiled into sugar

explanation.surface: An oddly worded question about whether we could get sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Would, say you' spoken gives 'wood': the clue asks which wood yields sugar, the Canadian tree tapped for syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree whose sap is boiled down into syrup and sugar.

clue.text: What made Rodin so worried at home?

indicators.note: worried letters are shaken and fretted about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about what upset the French sculptor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' shakes RODIN SO into a new order; 'What made' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inside one's house means being at home.

clue.text: Silver setting for Gaunt's precious stone

definitions.text: Silver setting for Gaunt's precious stone

parts.words: Silver setting for Gaunt's precious stone
parts.note: John of Gaunt in Richard II calls England 'this precious stone set in the silver' waters

explanation.surface: A jeweller's silver mount for a gem owned by a man named Gaunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's John of Gaunt praises England as 'this precious stone set in the silver sea'; the setting is the water round the island.
explanation.definitionFit: The waters surrounding England are the silver setting of Shakespeare's line.

clue.text: Ranch job for canon on horseback

parts.note: a canon in music is a round, voices entering in turn
a rider on a horse is said to be up

explanation.surface: Ranch work for a clergyman riding a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' suggests a clergyman, but it is the musical canon, a round.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering the cattle together is a key task on a ranch.

clue.text: Metric weight of a cask, some say

indicators.note: some speakers pronounce the cask word the same as the weight

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: What a barrel weighs in metric units, by one account.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand kilograms is the metric weight in question.

clue.text: Peer has yacht redesigned, original model

indicators.note: redesigned means the letters are given a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A nobleman has his boat redesigned from the first prototype.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is the original pattern from which copies are made.
